extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, academic peer reviewers (including early-career reviewers), researchers studying peer review, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesizing literature-derived standards and practical guidance for producing and assessing high-quality peer-review reports for academic journals. Covers reading strategies, manuscript-evaluation criteria, writing/report structure, tone, and meta-features of review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural components
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria pertaining to different sections and components of scientific writing (the IMRaD structure: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion). Reviewers are encouraged to perform a comprehensive, section-by-section evaluation from title to references and organize reviews by manuscript sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each manuscript section for its specific function; offer targeted feedback per section. A practical strategy is to assess the manuscript section by section and organize the review accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria related to writing and presentation that ensure clarity and ease of reading (grammar, coherent writing, organized presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear writing prevents ambiguities and improves credibility. Note grammar/typographical errors only when they hinder understanding; many journals instruct reviewers not to focus on spelling/grammar, but flag manuscripts that are unreadable. Coherent presentation makes it easier to navigate the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria related to the appropriateness and rigor of the study design and methods: rationale, alignment of hypothesis and methods, study design, sampling, data collection, and statistical analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the Methods section provides enough detail for replication. Evaluate whether experimental design and analyses are rigorous and suitable for testing the hypothesis; suggest better approaches if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific value
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria assessing the study's contribution to the field: contribution/new insights, significance/impact, novelty, and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work is original, offers new perspective, aligns with the journal mission, and has potential to change practice or open new research areas. Consider relevance and potential impact on practice or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for detecting and addressing ethical issues: data fabrication/falsification, plagiarism, approvals for human/animal research, conflicts of interest, and research bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report suspicions immediately to the editor. Verify ethical approvals and adherence to legal/ethical standards. Assess potential funding- or sponsor-induced bias. Use COPE guidelines as reference; reviewers play a key role in identifying ethical breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall criteria / suitability for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Global considerations about whether the manuscript fits the journal: alignment with mission, interest to readership, scope fit, and adherence to formatting/guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess topical relevance, how thoroughly the topic has been explored in recent literature, and whether the manuscript’s argument fits the journal’s scope. Check formatting and adherence to journal instructions as part of suitability assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reading — Pre-reading preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading, reviewers should understand the journal’s scope, audience, and specific requirements (e.g., 'Information for Authors' pages) and journal expectations for the review format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend a few minutes learning about the journal’s policies and preferred review format; ensure you have availability, relevant expertise, and no conflicts of interest before accepting a review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reading — Initial quick reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'quick read' to obtain a general understanding, determine manuscript type and study design, identify main objectives, and spot major flaws or reasons for summary rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the manuscript fits the journal’s scope and contributes to the field. If writing errors severely hinder understanding, suggest copyediting before detailed scientific evaluation. Use guiding questions: What are the objectives? Is the purpose consistent? Is the topic timely?

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reading — Critical reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough, detailed read focused on assessing scientific merit: relevance, importance, methodology, data, results, and possible improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: How relevant/important is this paper, and could it be improved? Use checklists per manuscript section to ensure necessary information is included. Suggest improvements to enhance clarity and scientific rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reading — Final review
rubrics_metrics.description: A final pass to capture remaining issues, verify abstract/title accuracy, and ensure feedback aligns with the overall recommendation (accept/revise/reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that comments are constructive and consistent with your recommendation. Reflect with questions such as: 'How would I feel if I received this review?' and ensure suggestions are clear and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading strategy — number of reads
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation on staged reading: commonly two or three readings (e.g., quick read, critical read, final read).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide tasks across readings: initial scope/fit and major-flaw detection; detailed evaluation and note-taking; final check for consistency and polish. Reviewers are encouraged to develop a reading style that suits them but many sources recommend structured multiple passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists / section-by-section evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ checklists to ensure coverage of required elements in each manuscript section and to reduce omission errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a checklist for each section helps ensure necessary information is included and supports systematic, reproducible reviews. Check title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments to author (content and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-facing comments should provide recommendations for improving the manuscript, emphasize strengths, point out shortcomings, and justify suggested decisions, but should not state the publication recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure comments to clarify the reviewer’s decision and help authors revise. Be supportive even when recommending rejection. Ensure comments to authors align with those given to the editor (substantively) but omit confidential evaluative statements or the final recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments to editor (content and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential section for editors that summarizes the reviewer’s overall assessment and provides rationale for acceptance/rejection/revision, plus any sensitive information the author should not see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise and objective; do not simply repeat author comments. Offer extra information to help editorial decision-making (e.g., concerns about misconduct, fit to journal, undisclosed conflicts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Desired qualities of language and attitude in review texts: fair, balanced, polite, civil, non-accusatory, professional, and constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate criticism professionally and respectfully. Avoid belittling or insulting authors. Be collegial; give constructive feedback kindly. Downplay excessive praise, and ensure a positive tone does not obscure identification of major flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and organization of the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize comments clearly and logically: brief overview of main strengths and weaknesses, section-structured critique, prioritized concerns, and clear separation of major vs minor issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number comments, divide into major and minor criticisms, and prioritize concerns to help authors and editors. A well-organized review facilitates systematic author rebuttals and editorial evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization of major vs minor issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish critical flaws that affect publication decisions from minor issues (e.g., typographical or formatting) so authors and editors know which items must be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate which problems could prevent publication and which are less critical. Numbered, prioritized lists improve clarity for revision and rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality features of peer review reports (core attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight essential quality features expected in review texts: 'constructive, specific, fair, thorough, courteous, consistent, objective, and readable feedback.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features summarize desirable report-level characteristics identified across the literature and should guide both writing and automated assessment of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Rooyen Review Quality Instrument (historical criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A foundational tool (Van Rooyen et al., 1999) based on eight criteria such as research question importance, originality, methodology, presentation, constructive feedback, substantiation, and result interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an early template for review-quality assessment; many later tools build on or vary these dimensions. Note: later studies identified many different tools and scales with 1–26 criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comments for editors vs authors (confidentiality practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly separate confidential commentary intended for editors from comments intended for authors, because the former may include sensitive assessments or judgments not appropriate for authors to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dedicated editor-comments field for overall recommendations and sensitive concerns (ethical issues, suspected misconduct, fit-for-journal judgments). Do not duplicate confidential reasoning in author-facing comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and exemplar comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing examples of good/poor review comments and model phrasing can guide reviewers towards higher-quality reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although fewer publications provide concrete examples, the literature recommends offering sample comments and templates to help reviewers structure feedback and adopt appropriate tone and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assessment and editorial monitoring tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors use various tools and scales to assess review quality (from single-item overall quality ratings to multi-criteria instruments), which affect whether reviewers remain in the pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instruments vary widely and can be prone to editorial bias and limited theoretical grounding. Awareness of how editors assess reviews should inform reviewers' focus (e.g., thoroughness, usefulness to editors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and transparent use of generative AI/LLMs in reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on using large language models and generative AI to assist review drafting and assessment, emphasizing ethical, transparent, and context-sensitive application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLMs can aid writing (e.g., tools like ReviewWriter) and generate assessments, but they have limitations (inconsistencies, inaccuracies). International committees recommend ethics and disclosure when LLMs are used; journals increasingly adopt context-specific policies.
